text: In June 1816, it snowed in New England.
Not a light frost. Snow — in the first week of summer — on fields that had just been planted.
In Europe, it rained for months. The harvest rotted. People ate moss, nettles and cats.
And in a villa on Lake Geneva, an eighteen-year-old stuck indoors by the storms started writing Frankenstein.
Nobody alive knew why. The cause was on the other side of the world — and it had happened a year earlier.
This is the story of the volcano that cancelled summer for the whole planet.
In April 1815, on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, a mountain called Tambora woke up.
The explosions were heard more than two thousand kilometres away. Soldiers on other islands thought it was cannon fire, and went looking for pirates.
It was the biggest eruption in recorded history. The mountain lost more than a kilometre of its height.
Around ten thousand people died in the eruption itself. Tens of thousands more died in the famine that followed on the islands nearby.
But the ash that fell on Sumbawa wasn't the dangerous part.
The dangerous part went up.

section: II. A veil around the Earth (1:45–2:35)
text: Tambora blew around sixty million tonnes of sulphur gas into the stratosphere — twenty, thirty, forty kilometres up.

section: II. A veil around the Earth (1:45–2:35)
text: Up there, there's no rain to wash it out. The gas turned into a haze of tiny droplets, and the winds spread it around the entire planet.

section: II. A veil around the Earth (1:45–2:35)
text: A veil, too thin to see — but thick enough to bounce sunlight back into space.

section: II. A veil around the Earth (1:45–2:35)
text: The whole Northern Hemisphere cooled by around half a degree. That sounds like nothing.

section: II. A veil around the Earth (1:45–2:35)
text: For farmers, it was everything.

section: III. Eighteen hundred and froze to death (2:35–3:40)
text: In New England, there was frost in every month of 1816. Corn froze in the fields in June, again in July, again in August.

section: III. Eighteen hundred and froze to death (2:35–3:40)
text: Americans gave the year a nickname: eighteen hundred and froze to death.

section: III. Eighteen hundred and froze to death (2:35–3:40)
text: Thousands of families gave up on New England altogether and moved west, to Ohio and beyond.

section: III. Eighteen hundred and froze to death (2:35–3:40)
text: In Europe it was worse. The price of wheat doubled. There were food riots in Britain and France. In Switzerland, people starved.

section: III. Eighteen hundred and froze to death (2:35–3:40)
text: In China's Yunnan province, the rice harvest failed. In India, the monsoon went wrong.

section: III. Eighteen hundred and froze to death (2:35–3:40)
text: Even horses went hungry — there were no oats. Some historians think that's why, the next year, a German inventor built a horse you didn't have to feed: the first bicycle.
Back on Lake Geneva, the storms kept a group of young English writers indoors for days.
Lord Byron, bored, challenged everyone to write a ghost story.
Mary Shelley came up with Frankenstein. Byron's doctor, John Polidori, wrote The Vampyre — the first modern vampire story.
Byron himself wrote a poem called Darkness — about the day the Sun goes out.
One cold summer gave us two of the most famous monsters in fiction.

section: V. The sky in the paintings (4:10–4:40)
text: And everywhere the veil went, the sunsets turned strange.

section: V. The sky in the paintings (4:10–4:40)
text: For years afterwards, the skies over Europe glowed blood red and orange.

section: V. The sky in the paintings (4:10–4:40)
text: Scientists have measured the colours in paintings from those years. After big eruptions, the painted sunsets really do get redder.
At the time, nobody connected any of this to a volcano on the other side of the world.
It took more than a century — until an American physicist named William Humphreys put the numbers together in 1920.
In 1991, we got to watch it happen again. Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines cooled the whole planet by about half a degree for two years.
Tambora threw out more than ten times as much rock as Pinatubo.
Volcanologists put the chance of another eruption that size this century at about one in six.
One in six. The same odds as rolling a die.
This time, at least, we'd know why the summer didn't come.
